extracted.intended_audience: educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and policymakers (K-12 and postsecondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for recipient grievance procedures under Title IX, including who may file complaints, required process elements (notice, investigation, hearings), limits on third-party filings, and when a Title IX Coordinator may initiate a complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt and equitable resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of sex discrimination complaints (language refined in §§106.46(a)(1) and 106.46(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes promptness has been a requirement since 1975 (see 34 CFR 106.8(c)) and avoiding unnecessary delay serves Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate; procedures should ensure timely resolution in the recipient's particular setting (elementary, secondary, postsecondary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance procedures must be in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: §§106.45(a)(1) and 106.46(a) require grievance procedures to be published in writing and to clearly explain a recipient's obligations under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written procedures inform recipients of obligations and provide clarity to all parties about required grievance processes; commenters supported this transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reliability in outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must include basic requirements to ensure transparency and reliability in outcomes for sex discrimination complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations enumerate provisions (see Employees—General Support and Opposition discussion) designed to ensure a fair process and reliable results; transparency includes clear notice, processes, and decision-making standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of conflicts of interest and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must adopt grievance procedures that address conflicts of interest and bias in decisionmakers and investigators (see §106.45(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should include safeguards to identify and mitigate conflicts and bias; the preamble cites this section as a core guarantee of a fair process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of allegations / written notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must provide notice of allegations, including written notice when required (see §106.45(c) and §106.46(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear written notice to parties is a required element to ensure understanding of allegations and to preserve fairness and due process in investigations and hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint investigation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must specify complaint investigation processes (see §§106.45(f) and 106.46(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should be structured, impartial, and follow the procedures set out in the regulations to support reliable fact-finding and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating allegations and assessing credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must include standards and processes for evaluating allegations and assessing witness/party credibility (see §§106.45(g) and 106.46(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sex-based harassment often involves contested factual disputes where credibility is central, procedures must guide evaluators in weighing evidence and credibility consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearings for postsecondary sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: For postsecondary sex-based harassment complaints, the regulations contemplate live hearings as part of the resolution process (see §106.46(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live hearings are recognized as appropriate in contested disputes where credibility determinations are critical; the regulations treat these differently than non-harassment sex discrimination matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must specify the standard of proof to be applied in determinations of responsibility (see §106.45(h)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble references this as a key procedural element; recipients must set and apply a clear standard consistently across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural protections tailored to context
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural protections must account for the age, maturity, and level of independence of students, the contexts of employees and third parties, and the need to ensure prompt and equitable resolution in particular settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations provide procedural protections appropriate to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary settings and consider different participant roles (students, employees, third parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: complaints need not involve a named respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures are not limited to complaints that involve a complainant and an individual respondent; complaints against a recipient's policy or practice can trigger grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some provisions of §106.45 may not apply to policy/practice complaints, but recipients must implement those parts that do apply; this avoids limiting remedies to interpersonal disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient is not a 'respondent' when complaint challenges recipient policy/practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complaint challenges the recipient's policy or practice, the recipient is not considered a respondent and is not entitled to certain procedural rights afforded individual respondents under §§106.45/106.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that individual respondent procedural protections do not automatically extend to institutional defendants, but recipients remain bound to implement applicable parts of §106.45; recipients may still be protected from discrimination as parties in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make a complaint — general rule for non-harassment claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For sex discrimination other than sex-based harassment, a complaint may be filed by: (a) any student or employee; (b) any person other than a student or employee who was participating or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity at the time of the alleged sex discrimination; (c) a complainant, parent/guardian/legal representative; or (d) the Title IX Coordinator in limited circumstances (§106.45(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.45(a)(2)(iv) to split (A) any student or employee and (B) any non-student/non-employee who was participating or attempting to participate at the time; the qualifier about participation applies only to non-students/non-employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on who may file sex-based harassment complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A sex-based harassment complaint may only be filed by: the complainant (a person alleged to have been subjected to sex discrimination), a parent/guardian/authorized legal representative with the legal right to act on behalf of the complainant, or, in limited circumstances, the Title IX Coordinator (§§106.45(a)(2)(i)-(iii), 106.44(f)(1)(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limitation is designed to protect complainant autonomy given the deeply personal nature of harassment allegations; it differs from the broader filing rules for other types of sex discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant autonomy preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations restrict third-party initiation of sex-based harassment complaints to protect the complainant's autonomy over whether to request initiation of grievance procedures (except where the Title IX Coordinator must act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy balances encouraging reporting with protecting complainants' control; commenters supported preserving autonomy and the rule limits third-party filings for harassment claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator limited initiation authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX Coordinator may initiate a complaint without a complainant only after determining the alleged conduct presents an imminent and serious threat to health or safety of a complainant or other person, or that the conduct prevents the recipient from ensuring equal access based on sex to its education program or activity (§106.44(f)(1)(v)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiation by the Title IX Coordinator is not broad or presumptive; it is constrained to fact-specific determinations and requires consideration of enumerated factors (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors the Title IX Coordinator must consider before initiating
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to initiate without a complainant, the Title IX Coordinator must consider, at minimum, the factors listed in §106.44(f)(1)(v)(A)(1)-(8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors include: (1) the complainant's request not to proceed; (2) the complainant's reasonable safety concerns about initiation; (3) risk that additional acts would occur if not initiated; (4) severity of the alleged sex discrimination, including whether removal/discipline might be necessary; (5) age and relationship of the parties, including whether respondent is an employee; (6) scope of the alleged discrimination, including patterns or impacts on multiple individuals; (7) availability of evidence to assist a decisionmaker; and (8) whether the recipient could end the alleged discrimination and prevent recurrence without initiating the grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bystander filing limits for sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who observes an incident may file a complaint only if the incident creates a hostile environment for that person; uninvolved bystanders with no connection to the institution may not file sex-based harassment complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harassment law recognizes that individuals may experience a hostile environment even if not the direct target; the rule prevents filings by people with no personal connection to the recipient or alleged hostile environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No separate 'standing' requirement for third-party complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to add a separate standing requirement for third-party complaints because Title IX complaints are resolved by educational entities rather than courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the regulations limit who may file to individuals with some relationship to the recipient to mitigate speculative complaints; the statutory phrase 'no person' supports broad protection within the educational community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of complaints of sex discrimination other than harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'complaints of sex discrimination other than sex-based harassment' includes allegations such as retaliation (§106.71), failures to make reasonable modifications (§106.40(b)(3)(ii)), or claims that a recipient's policy or procedures discriminate on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These types of claims often implicate policies/practices or community-wide harms and therefore justify broader reporting options than sex-based harassment claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with case law and constitutional protections; agency authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determines that §§106.45 and 106.46 are within its authority under 20 U.S.C. 1682, consistent with applicable case law, and interpreted consistent with the U.S. Constitution (§106.6(d) preserves constitutional rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains the Department examined relevant case law and maintains the procedures align with authority and precedent; where state or local law conflicts with these federal regulations, the federal provisions preempt conflicting state/local law.
